subject: Math

The ball is above the box. Is it below the box?
No. It is above the box.

Put your hand above your head.

position-two
Put one hand beside your head and one above it.
Teacher checks: one hand is beside the head and the other is above it.

Where is the bear compared with the chair?

Lay two unequal strips with their starting ends offset.

4 crayons.

3 counters.

Make up an adding story for 3 + 4.

needs-sort-check
Someone put water in the “plants only” group. Where should water go instead?
Water belongs in the shared-needs group because plants and animals both need water.

Tired.

subject: Literacy

To fly her kite.

Write 52,406 in expanded form.

add-money

Cause: the bus left before Leo arrived. Effect: Leo walked.

cause-unsupported
“Lena smiled when she opened the envelope.” Does this sentence prove she received money? Explain using only the text.
No. It says she smiled and opened an envelope, but does not tell what was inside.

subject: Literacy
evidence: I can use details from the text to identify and explain the main idea.
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: main-topic
Our class reads poems, writes poems, and shares poems. What is this text mostly about?
The class’s work with poems.
main-detail
The club keeps the park clean. Members pick up litter and empty bins. Give the main idea and one supporting detail.
Main idea: the club keeps the park clean. Detail: members pick up litter or empty bins.
main-revise
The library lends books, offers story time, and hosts reading clubs. Is “The library only lends books” a good main idea? Explain and improve it.
No; “only” leaves out the other activities. Better: the library offers several ways to read and enjoy books.
main-title
“We mend torn books and replace broken covers.” Choose a title: Caring for Books or Fixing Covers.
Caring for Books. Fixing covers is only one detail.
main-unrelated
A paragraph explains how students care for a garden. Which detail belongs: students water the seedlings, or the garden has a wooden fence?
Students water the seedlings. The fence is about the garden, not about caring for it.
main-build
A class labels supply bins, assigns shelf spaces, and returns tools after use. Write a main-idea sentence supported by all three details.
The class keeps its supplies organized. Accept another main idea that covers all three details.

subject: Science
evidence: I can collect, record, and analyze weather, cloud, and moon phase data to identify patterns and explain changes over time.
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: weather-read
Our chart says Monday: sunny; Tuesday: cloudy. What weather was recorded Tuesday?
Cloudy.
weather-compare
Cloud-cover notes: Monday clear, Tuesday partly cloudy, Wednesday fully cloudy. Describe the change.
The recorded cloud cover increased from clear to partly cloudy to fully cloudy.
weather-limits
One day was rainy. Is that enough data to show a repeating weekly weather pattern? Explain.
No. One observation cannot show repetition; collect observations across more days and weeks.
weather-frequency
Rain was recorded on Monday and Friday, but not the other weekdays. How many weekdays were rainy?
2 weekdays.
weather-data-gap
A chart has weather entries for Monday and Wednesday. Which missing weekday entry would complete that three-day record?
Tuesday.
weather-comparison-fair
One cloud chart records noon each day; another records different times. Which makes a clearer same-time comparison across days? Explain.
The noon chart keeps observation time consistent, making changes across days easier to compare.

subject: Math
section: Aug 24–28, Whole Number Operations and Applications
evidence: I can find the volume of a rectangular prism by counting cubes or using a formula.
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: volume-cubes
A solid is built from 18 unit cubes, with no gaps or overlaps. What is its volume?
18 cubic units.
volume-layers
A rectangular prism has 4 layers, with 6 unit cubes in each layer. What is its volume?
24 cubic units.
volume-dimensions
A rectangular prism is 5 units long, 3 units wide, and 2 units high. Find its volume and explain.
30 cubic units: 5 × 3 × 2 = 30. Each of two layers has 15 unit cubes.
volume-unit
Jo counts the cubes that fill a prism and gets 24. Which label fits: 24 units or 24 cubic units?
24 cubic units.
volume-compare
Prism A has 3 layers of 8 cubes. Prism B has 2 layers of 12 cubes. Which has greater volume, or are they equal?
They are equal: each has 24 cubic units.
volume-error
For a 4 by 3 by 2 prism, Jo adds 4 + 3 + 2 and says its volume is 9. Explain why this does not count the cubes correctly.
Each layer has 4 × 3 = 12 cubes, and there are 2 layers. The volume is 24 cubic units; adding the edge lengths does not count the cubes.

subject: Math
evidence: I can multiply multi-digit whole numbers using place value strategies and the standard algorithm.
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: multiply-ten
What is 34 × 10?
multiply-partial
Find 23 × 14 using partial products.
multiply-error
A student writes 42 × 13 = 42 × 10 + 42 × 2. What is wrong? Find the correct product.
13 = 10 + 3, not 10 + 2. The correct product is 420 + 126 = 546.
multiply-hundred
Complete the product: 21 × 100.
multiply-area-parts
To compute 36 × 12, the first partial product is 360. What is the other partial product and the total?
72; total 432.
multiply-estimate-check
Someone says 48 × 21 = 148. Explain why that is too small, then calculate the product.
Even 48 × 20 is 960, so 148 is too small. 960 + 48 = 1,008.

subject: Literacy
evidence: I can analyze the use of narrative techniques to present ideas, design texts, and convey information about characters, setting, and plot. (5.T.T.1.a)
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: setting-evidence
“At dawn, Jo waited beside the school gate.” Identify the setting details.
Time: dawn. Place: beside the school gate.
character-action
“Even after missing three shots, Maya kept practicing.” What does this action suggest about Maya? Cite evidence.
She is persistent or determined; she keeps practicing after missing three shots.
dialogue-inference
“I can’t wait!” Ari exclaimed, bouncing in his seat. How do the words and actions work together to reveal his feelings?
Both suggest excitement or eagerness: “I can’t wait” and bouncing in his seat support that inference.
narrative-dialogue
“Please stay,” Eva said. Which words are the character’s spoken dialogue?
Please stay.
narrative-setting-effect
“In the dark hallway, Ren felt along the wall for the switch.” How does the setting explain Ren’s action?
The hallway is dark, so Ren feels for the switch instead of relying on sight.
narrative-contrast
“I am not worried,” Sol said, gripping the chair tightly. How might the dialogue and action suggest different feelings?
The words deny worry, but gripping tightly may suggest tension or worry. Accept an interpretation supported by both details.

subject: Literacy
evidence: I can explain how a character changes and how that shows the theme of the story. (5.T.T.1.c)
timingBasis: Main pacing-guide subject row and linked document section agree for this skill/date. Only the quoted skill is used; extra linked standards are not added to the main mapping.
questions: character-change
At first, Lee refused help. Later, Lee asked a friend for help. What changed?
Lee changed from refusing help to accepting or asking for it.
theme-help
Sam tried alone and struggled. After asking for help, Sam succeeded. What possible theme does this suggest?
Asking for help can help us succeed. Accept another theme supported by the events.
theme-evidence
Rae hid every mistake. After a friend shared a mistake, Rae admitted one and learned from it. Explain a possible theme using Rae’s change.
Being honest about mistakes can help us learn. Rae changes from hiding mistakes to admitting one and learning from it.
change-end
At first, Pat quit when a puzzle was hard. By the end, Pat tried again. What does Pat do differently at the end?
Pat keeps trying instead of quitting.
theme-sharing
Dee kept all the supplies and could not finish alone. Later, Dee shared and the group finished together. Suggest a supported theme.
Sharing and working together can help people succeed. Accept another theme supported by the events.
theme-reject
Jo mocked a beginner, then struggled with a new skill and became kinder. Does “Winning is everything” fit Jo’s change? Explain a better theme.
No. A better theme is that experiencing difficulty can help us understand and treat others kindly; Jo changes from mocking to kindness.
